Reference stored intersections SYMBOLICALLY in written setups — 'where X₁ = 0.7531 is the positive intersection' — then use full precision in the machine. The written decimal is for the reader; the stored value is for the arithmetic. Two audiences, two precisions.

sections.title: Inverse and Solver Problems
sections.subtitle: When the unknown is a bound
sections.body:
The section's thinking questions invert the formulas: 'find k so the line y = k divides R into two regions of equal area' sets ∫(condition with k) = (half the total) and solves numerically for k. The integral becomes a FUNCTION of the unknown — area-so-far as a function of the divider — and the equation solver does the rest. FTC thinking (accumulation as a function of its bound) is the conceptual engine; the machine is the wrench.

The family: equal-area dividers (horizontal or vertical lines), equal-volume planes (last chapter's x = c slicer), unknown endpoints ('the curve from 0 to b has length 5'), and parameter-tuning ('find a so the area equals 3'). Each writes one equation in one unknown where the equation CONTAINS an integral; each is two written lines (the equation, the numerical solution) plus solver work.

Setup language for the rubric: 'Let A(k) = ∫... ; solve A(k) = 4.519/2' — the equation visibly stated, the unknown named, the numerical answer to three decimals. The statement of the equation is the point-bearing artifact; the solving is assumed competent.

A worked instance: R under y = 4 - x² above the axis (area 32/3). Find k with the horizontal line y = k splitting R equally. Area above y = k: the region between the curve and the line, ∫(4 - x² - k) dx over where 4 - x² ≥ k, which integrates (by symmetry and substitution) to (4/3)(4 - k)^{3/2}. Equation: (4/3)(4 - k)^{3/2} = 16/3, so (4 - k)^{3/2} = 4, 4 - k = 4^{2/3}, k = 4 - 4^{2/3} ≈ 1.480. Clean enough by hand here — but the SHAPE of the work (area-as-function, one equation, solve) is the calculator section's daily bread.
key_terms: The unknown lives in a bound or parameter; the solver finishes
'Solve A(k) = total/2' written out is the graded move
Equal areas, equal volumes, target lengths, tuned parameters
boxes: ap_alert

Equal-division problems: compute the TOTAL first, then set the partial accumulation equal to half of it. Solving 'left = right' directly (two integrals, one equation) also works but doubles the setup; total-then-half is the cleaner graded line.

sections.title: The Unit, Banked
sections.subtitle: Formulas, audits, and the bridge to Unit 9
sections.body:
The unit's formula bank, final inventory: average value (1/(b-a))∫f; position s(t₀) + ∫v; displacement ∫v; distance ∫|v|; area ∫(top - bottom) or ∫(right - left); volume ∫A(x) with the shape catalog; disks π∫r²; washers π∫(R² - r²); arc length ∫√(1 + (y')²). Nine entries, every one an instance of chop-measure-sum, every one tested.

The audits, banked beside them: units (linear/square/cubic matching the formula's dimension); positivity (areas, distances, lengths, volumes are positive — negatives flag order errors); the chord check (arc ≥ straight-line distance); the anchor check (positions need initial values); three decimals, rounded last.

What transfers to Unit 9 immediately: the particle goes planar — position (x(t), y(t)), velocity as a vector, speed √((x')² + (y')²), distance as the parametric arc length. Areas reappear under polar curves with a new slicing geometry (sectors, not rectangles): A = (1/2)∫r² dθ. The chop-measure-sum habit converts both formulas from memorization into re-derivation.

The course's geography from here: Unit 9 (parametric, polar, vectors — BC's geometry unit) and Unit 10 (series — BC's capstone) remain. Both are BC-only territory, both lean on everything banked so far, and together they carry roughly 30% of the BC exam's weight. The applied integral toolkit is complete; what remains is teaching it new coordinate systems and then infinite sums.
key_terms: Average value through arc length: the unit's complete tested inventory
Units, positivity, chord, anchor, three decimals — five checks, most errors
Planar particles and polar sectors: the same habits, new geometry
boxes: ap_alert

The calculator section rewards a fixed pre-flight: MODE radians; intersections stored; setups written before typing; three decimals at the end. Four habits, rehearsed until boring — they are collectively worth more points than any single formula in the bank.

choices.C: the calculator is in degree mode

mcq.explanation: Areas are positive; a negative result means the subtraction ran upside down. The positivity audit caught it.

frq.question:
Let R be the region bounded by y = e^{-x²} and y = x² (calculator active).
(a) Find the x-coordinates of the intersection points to three decimals, and state how they should be handled in later parts.
(b) Find the area of R.
(c) Set up, but do not evaluate, the volume of the solid generated when R is revolved about the line y = 2.
rubric: (a) e^{-x²} = x² at x ≈ ±0.753 (stored, used at full precision)
(c) Axis above: R_outer = 2 - x², r_inner = 2 - e^{-x²}
frq.model_answer: (a) Solving e^{-x²} = x² numerically: x ≈ ±0.753 (more precisely 0.7531...). The roots are stored in calculator variables and used at full precision in every later integral; the written 0.753 is for the reader only. (b) The exponential rides above the parabola between the roots: A = ∫_{-X₁}^{X₁} (e^{-x²} - x²) dx = 2∫₀^{X₁} (e^{-x²} - x²) dx ≈ 1.038. (c) The axis y = 2 sits ABOVE the region, so the curve closer to it — the exponential — gives the SMALLER radius: outer R = 2 - x², inner r = 2 - e^{-x²}. V = π∫_{-X₁}^{X₁} [(2 - x²)² - (2 - e^{-x²})²] dx — complete as a setup.

frq.question:
A particle moves along the x-axis with velocity v(t) = t·cos(t²) - 0.2 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 3, starting at x(0) = 1 (calculator active).
(a) Find the particle's position at t = 3.
(b) Find the total distance traveled on [0, 3].
(c) Find the time in (0, 3) at which the particle is farthest LEFT, with justification.
rubric: (a) x(3) = 1 + ∫₀³ v dt ≈ 1 + (-0.675) ≈ 0.325 (machine value; accept ≈ 0.32–0.33 with setup)
(b) ∫₀³ |v(t)| dt, numerically (≈ 1.99; accept with correct setup)
(c) Candidates where v changes − to + (numerically locate sign changes of v); compare x at candidates and endpoints
Justification: position minimal where v flips − to +, values compared via accumulation
frq.model_answer: (a) x(3) = x(0) + ∫₀³ v(t) dt = 1 + ∫₀³ (t cos(t²) - 0.2) dt — machine evaluation of the integral gives ≈ -0.675, so x(3) ≈ 0.325. (b) Total distance = ∫₀³ |v(t)| dt, entered with abs() and evaluated numerically: ≈ 1.99. (c) The particle is farthest left at a time where v changes sign from negative to positive (a local minimum of position) or at an endpoint. Solving v(t) = 0 numerically locates the sign changes; computing x at each candidate via x(0) + ∫₀^c v dt and comparing with x(0) = 1 and x(3) ≈ 0.325 identifies the global minimum. The justification sentence — 'x is minimized where v changes from negative to positive, and the accumulated positions at the candidates compare as...' — plus the numeric comparison completes the answer. (Exact candidate values depend on the machine solve; the method is the graded content.)

frq.question:
Let R be the region under y = 4 - x² and above the x-axis.
(a) Compute the total area of R exactly.
(b) Find the value k such that the horizontal line y = k divides R into two regions of equal area. (The area of the part of R ABOVE y = k equals (4/3)(4 - k)^{3/2}.)
(c) Verify your k numerically by evaluating the upper area, and explain why k is NOT simply 2 (half the height).
rubric: Not 2: area distributes by the region's WIDTH, which is greatest near the bottom — the halving line sits below mid-height
frq.model_answer: (a) A = ∫₋₂² (4 - x²) dx = 2(8 - 8/3) = 32/3. (b) Set the upper area to half the total: (4/3)(4 - k)^{3/2} = 16/3, so (4 - k)^{3/2} = 4, 4 - k = 4^{2/3}, k = 4 - 4^{2/3} ≈ 1.480. (c) Check: (4/3)(4 - 1.480)^{3/2} = (4/3)(2.520)^{3/2} ≈ (4/3)(4.000) = 16/3 ✓. And k ≠ 2 because area is not distributed evenly in height: the parabolic region is WIDE near its base and narrow near its peak, so the lower half of the height holds more than half the area — the equal-area line must sit below y = 2 to give the top piece enough room. Geometry weights by width; the integral knows.
